competency_fulfillment.rationale: Every one of the fourteen samples is a worded problem that resolves to a perimeter, which is precisely what solving problems involving perimeter asks. Seed 603 'A triangular flower bed has sides 3 cm, 9 cm, and 11 cm. How much edging is needed to go all the way around it?' gives 23, seed 500 'A square garden has a side of 17 cm. How much fencing is needed to go all the way around it?' gives 68, and seed 604 'A rectangular garden is 4 cm long and 7 cm wide.' gives 22. All fourteen answers are correct and each is answerable from its own stem. This node is clearly distinguished from its siblings: the shape is always named adjectivally inside a situation and the question asks for fencing or edging rather than naming perimeter outright, so the student must recognise which measure the situation calls for.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: All three named shapes are present in context. Triangular at seeds 42, 501, 502 and 603, for instance seed 501 'A triangular flower bed has sides 10 cm, 21 cm, and 17 cm.'; square at seeds 44, 45, 50, 500 and 600, for instance seed 600 'A square garden has a side of 6 cm.'; rectangular at seeds 43, 46, 601, 604 and 605, for instance seed 43 'A rectangular garden is 5 cm long and 12 cm wide.'. Every triangle can exist under the triangle inequality: seed 42 'A triangular flower bed has sides 2 cm, 1 cm, and 2 cm.' has 1+2>2, seed 501 has 10+17>21, seed 502 'A triangular flower bed has sides 12 cm, 6 cm, and 17 cm.' has 6+12=18>17, and seed 603 has 3+9=12>11, so all four are constructible figures.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Each problem is one step once the situation is read: add three sides or double a sum, on whole centimetres with answers from 5 to 68. The sentences are short and concrete, one situation per item, no extraneous numbers, and no conversion. Seed 45 'A square garden has a side of 7 cm. How much fencing is needed to go all the way around it?' shows the ceiling of the reading load, which is appropriate for grade 2 quarter 4.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Two formatters appear (mcq at seed 604, cloze at seeds 50, 500, 601 and 605), all three shapes recur, and the context verb varies with the shape, edging for the flower beds and fencing for the gardens, as in 'How much edging is needed to go all the way around it?' at seed 502 against 'How much fencing is needed to go all the way around it?' at seed 600. Side values range from 1 to 21 and cover isosceles and scalene triangles, squares and both orientations of rectangle.

competency_alignment.rationale: Nothing exceeds the sentence and nothing falls short. No item asks for area, for a missing side from a known perimeter, for a comparison of two figures, or for a shape beyond triangles, squares and rectangles, and none degenerates into a bare computation drill: every stem is a situation, for example seed 46 'A rectangular garden is 7 cm long and 1 cm wide. How much fencing is needed to go all the way around it?'.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: The numbers suit grade 2 but the unit does not suit any object named, and this holds for all fourteen samples rather than a stray one. Seed 43 'A rectangular garden is 5 cm long and 12 cm wide.' and seed 601 'A rectangular garden is 4 cm long and 11 cm wide.' describe gardens smaller than a sheet of paper; seed 603 'A triangular flower bed has sides 3 cm, 9 cm, and 11 cm.' is a flower bed a student could cover with one hand; seed 46 'A rectangular garden is 7 cm long and 1 cm wide.' is a strip one centimetre across that no fence could enclose. Metres are the plausible unit for gardens and flower beds at every one of these values. Two further stems describe a garden as longer in width than in length, seed 43 and seed 604 'A rectangular garden is 4 cm long and 7 cm wide.', which reads oddly against the word long. The perimeter arithmetic is correct throughout; the defect is that every context in the pool is modelled at centimetre scale.
